paper_title: VibeVideoBench: Evaluating Multimodal Agents on Code-Driven Video Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Diffusion video models produce striking clips, but they cannot reliably render an exact formula, a correct chart, a rule-consistent game or narration synchronized to on-screen events. A different route is emerging: multimodal agents that write code to render every frame and synthesize every sound. We introduce VibeVideoBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents on code-driven video generation. Its 239 self-contained tasks in English and Chinese span 12 categories, from data stories and music-driven pieces to classroom lessons and paper explainers; each asks an agent, running in its native harness inside a sandbox with no image or video generation model, to deliver a finished MP4 with sound within one hour. Evaluation is hierarchical and evidence-based: program checks of the delivery spec, about 13k task-specific rubric checks traced to the requirements they enforce, and five quality dimensions anchored per task, scored by three VLM judge panels. Across nine frontier agent systems and 2,151 scored rollouts, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 rank first and second with both the judges and human annotators, and the strongest system satisfies every core requirement on 76.3% of tasks. Delivery is a second axis: counting missing videos as zero changes the ranking, and three quarters of the lost videos are final renders that started too late, ran too slowly or never started, a failure of how agents plan their hour. Agents build their own rendering pipelines and inspect their own frames, yet how much they look does not predict quality. The judges' ranking of the systems closely matches blind human preferences.

Introduction Video generation has advanced rapidly through diffusion transformers [7, 21, 32, 45, 51, 56], and benchmarks such as VBench [27, 59] and EvalCrafter [36] measure how plausible and prompt-aligned the generated clips look. Yet many of the videos people actually makeclassroom lessons, paper explainers, data stories, product walkthroughs, assembly sequences, rhythm gamesdemand properties that pixel generators do not guarantee: exact text and numbers, rule-consistent state changes, multi-minute structure, sound aligned to events, and an artifact that can be revised. These are natural properties of programs. Humans already make such videos with Manim or Remotion, and coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex [1, 41] can now work autonomously for hours, driving full toolchaina renderer, headless browser, TTS engine, ffmpegon their own. Users have begun to ask agents for finished videos this way, which requires multimodal agent that reads input assets, produces picture and sound through code, and inspects its own renders to correct them. How good are agents at making videos? Existing evaluations do not answer this. Video-generation benchmarks score short, silent clips from generative models [24, 27, 36]. Codeto-visual benchmarks score single programs or static artifacts such as charts, web pages and SVGs [11, 48, 49, 58]. Codebased lesson and paper-to-video systems [12, 33, 63] are language-model pipelines: workflow designed by hand for one domain and one renderer, in which model is called at preset steps; they do not test general agents. Agentic benchmarks [30, 38, 54] verify textual or functional outcomes with unit tests, whereas video is perceptual, temporal and audio-visual outcome for which no unit test exists. Video therefore tests what text-only agentic benchmarks cannot: whether an agent can check its own output across picture, sound and time. We present VibeVideoBench (Figs. 1 and 2), benchmark that evaluates multimodal agents end to end on codedriven video generation: given specification and optional input assets, an agent must deliver finished MP4, built entirely with code, inside sandbox within one hour, with narration, music and sound effects as each tasks audio policy specifies. Every frame is rendered by code: no image or video generation model is available, and the only generative tool is TTS. Its 239 tasks span 12 categories, from data stories and music-driven pieces to classroom lessons and paper explainers, in English and Chinese. Three design choices shape it. Tasks must be realistic yet checkable. Real requests are open-ended, vague and often missing the content they refer to, so they cannot be checked as written. We build tasks from four sourcesreal user requests to code-video tools (rewritten), real videos (seeded from their dense captions), real asset packs such as 3D scans and game levels, and lecture notes and research papersand rewrite each into self-contained specification that fixes facts, identities, stages, timing and the audio policy while preserving creative freedom. Evaluation must rest on evidence in the video. video has no unit test, holistic score cannot be traced to evidence, judge may credit result the video merely claims, and many VLMs cannot hear. Evaluation therefore has three layers with different executors. Program checks (L1) automatically verify the delivery specresolution, frame rate, duration, audible sound, source project. Rubric checks (L2; about 13k in total) are each traced to the requirement they enforce, separate process shown from result claimed, and are tagged by modality. Quality scores (L3) rate five dimensionsvisual quality, aesthetics, content logic, timing and audioeach anchored at 1, 3 and 5 by descriptions written for the task. L2 and L3 are judged by VLM judges in three independent panels: two watch the full video with sound, and the third routes visual checks to vision model and audio checks to an audio-capable model, so audio checks never reach judge that cannot hear. Agents are evaluated as they are deployed. Users adopt model together with its harness, yet fair comparison needs identical conditions. Each model therefore runs fully autonomously in its vendors native harness at the highest effort its provider accepts, with no follow-up turns and all tool permissions pre-approved, in identical containers with the same one-hour budget; we evaluate complete agent systems rather than separating model from harness. Nine frontier systems from six labs yield 2,151 scored rollouts. Findings. (1) The benchmark is far from solved, and two systems lead. GPT-6 Astra [43] and Claude Opus 5.5 [2] rank first and second with both the judges and human annotators, yet even the best system satisfies every core requirement on only 76.3% of tasks. (2) Delivery is second axis. Counting missing videos as zero changes the ranking markedly: Gemini 4 Argon [20] delivers only 77% of its videos and falls from 4th to 7th. (3) Videos are lost to how agents use their time. Of the 224 runs without playable video, 169 are final renders that started too late, ran too slowly to finish before the deadline (e.g., frame-by-frame browser capture) or never started; Opus, the only system without failure, finishes median of 24 minutes before the deadline. (4) Agents build their own renderers, and self-inspection is universal but not decisive. Each system keeps house rendering stack (cairo, PIL/numpy, or browser canvases and three.js); 95% of runs view their own frames, but how much they look does not predict quality (ρ=0.07), and final reports often claim verifications that do not hold. (5) Judges are reliable for ranking systems, not single videos. The mean of the three panels ranks systems as humans do (ρ=0.98), but agrees with humans on only 73% of individual pairs (5). Our contributions are: 2 VibeVideoBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark of general multimodal agents on open-domain code-driven video generation with audio: 239 tasks in 12 categories (English and Chinese), about 13k task-specific rubric checks, each traced to the requirement it enforces, input assets and reproducible sandbox (3, Tab. 1). hierarchical, evidence-based evaluation protocol: program checks of the delivery spec, rubric checks that separate process shown from result claimed, and quality scores anchored per task, judged by three independent panels with modality routing so that audio checks reach only judges that can hear; missing videos are handled explicitly by reporting both delivered-only and no-video-as-zero results (4). large-scale empirical study of nine frontier agent systems from six labs (2,151 scored rollouts, 6.5k video judgments), with run-by-run analysis of all 224 failed deliveries, trajectory-level analysis of how agents make videos (renderers, self-inspection, delivery timing), and blind pairwise human preference study on all 239 tasks (5). 2. Related Work Video generation: the pixel paradigm. Diffusiontransformer generators [7, 21, 34, 51] synthesize pixels directly from text or images and are evaluated by dimensionlearned scorers [24], physics wise suites [27, 36, 59], probes [5, 37] and arenas [28]; VideoArgus [57], closest in spirit to our rubric checks, builds sample-specific rubrics before seeing outputs. Story-video systems [35, 53] add an LLM planner, but generative model still paints the pixels. We study different paradigm, in which an agent produces video by writing programs that drive renderers, TTS and ffmpeg, so that content is exact, editable, and controllable in length and sound. Evaluation that asks whether few seconds of mostly silent footage look plausible does not transfer to it. Code as visual medium: the program paradigm. Programs are an editable, verifiable visual representation of charts, web pages, SVG and 3D scenes [11, 22, 48, 49]; ArtifactsBench [58] grades interactive artifacts from screenshots with checklist-guided MLLM judges. For video, TheoremExplainAgent [33], Code2Video [12], VisualEDU [10] and ManimAgent [29] generate educational Manim videos, Paper2Video [63] turns research papers into narrated slide talks, and an industry benchmark [25] scores short silent clips written in one framework. Code2Video-Compass [13] evaluates language models rather than agents: each video is code written in single model call, without execution feedback or repair, and has no sound. None of these is agentic in our sense: each video comes from language-model pipeline built around one renderer or genre, or from single model call, rather than from an agent that chooses its own tools and renders, inspects and revises its own video. Table 1. Positioning. Among the benchmarks we know of, only VibeVideoBench has general-purpose agents build complete audiovisual videos from scratch with code across open domains, graded with task-specific rubrics. : yes; : no; : partially. Software and computer-use agents are measured by SWE-bench [30], Terminal-Bench [38], OSWorld [54] and PaperBench [50], and GDPval [44] grades occupational deliverables by expert comparison. These verify text, files or functional behavior, whereas video is perceptual, temporal and audio-visual outcome for which no unit test exists. AgenticVBench [8] also runs general agents in vendor harnesses, but on post-production of given footage; in our setting every frame and sound must be constructed by code. Tab. 1 contrasts VibeVideoBench with prior work on who makes the video, what is asked, what is delivered and how it is graded. Judges, rubrics and human preference. LLM and multimodal judges [9, 31, 60] exhibit position and self-preference biases [52] (we test self-preference in App. D.4); rubric decomposition improves reliability in non-verifiable domains [4, 23], and pairwise human preference with Bradley Terry aggregation [6, 14] is the standard validation. Omni models can see and hear [55], but audio-visual benchmarks show they remain weak at fine temporal alignment [17, 26]. We therefore route checks by modality, require timestamped evidence, use three independent panels, and measure where they fail. 3. VibeVideoBench 3.1. Task formulation task τ = (p, A, d, a, c) consists of natural-language specification p, an optional read-only asset package (data, fonts, sprites, 3D scans, audio), machine-readable delivery spec (resolution, frame rate, duration range [tmin, tmax], optional exact frame count), an audio policy that marks each of four channelsnarration, music, sound effects, ambienceas required, optional or not used, and an explicit creative-freedom statement c. An agent receives (p, A, d, a, c) in fresh container and must deliver video v, an editable source project and timing sheet before the deadline. There is no ground-truth video: deliverable is judged only against the frozen specification, and any rendering stack is allowed. No imageor video-generation model is 3 Figure 2. Overview of VibeVideoBench. (a) Tasks seeded from four kinds of real-world sources are drafted under shared contract, given the assets they need (searched for or synthesized by an LLM), and curated by humans, yielding benchmark that is diverse in content, form, length and sound. (b) Each task gets three-level rubric traced to its prompt and its input assets; L2 checks quote their basis and carry modality tags; rubrics go through rounds of model review and human review until no flag holds. (c) Agents run in native harnesses in identical one-hour sandboxes; programs check L1, and three VLM judge panelsone routing each check by modalityscore L2 and L3. provided; the only generative service is TTS command-line tool backed by Qwen3-TTS-Flash [46]. from 8 to 15 min, with narration, music, effects and ambience, with or without input assets  (Fig. 3)  . 3.2. Task construction 3.3. Statistics Fig. 2a shows the pipeline. Sources. Tasks start from four kinds of real-world sources: requests people wrote for codebased video tools (what people ask for), dense captions of real videos (what people actually make), real asset packs such as 3D scans, archival records and game sprites, and lecture notes and research papers. Specification contract. Real requests are rarely self-contained, so source only seeds task: LLM drafters with cross-review expand and rewrite it under shared contract that fixes every fact, number and object identity the video depends on, divides it into stages with dwell times and states four-channel audio policy, while protecting creative freedom; missing assets are searched for or synthesized. What the contract fixes can be checked, and what it leaves open measures the agents own design. Human curation. Humans select checkable tasks over open briefs, rewrite each into self-contained prompt without authoring traces, verify its facts and remove duplicates across sources. The result is 239 tasks in 12 categories and 43 subcategories, Fig. 3 summarizes the benchmark (App. A). Each task has one of 12 categories (content and purpose) and one or more of 43 subcategories, which cut across categories: 34 presentation forms (e.g., mechanism and causal chain, worked examples, map journeys) and 9 knowledge domains (e.g., mathematics, physics, AI). 209 tasks are in English and 30 in Chinese; 201 ship input assets (median 7 files; 2.7 GB); 70% require at least one audio channel and 49% require speech; most require 19201080 at 30 fps, 54 an exact frame count. One pass asks for 11.1 hours of finished video. 3.4. Rubrics Fig. 2b shows how rubrics are built. Every check traces to the final prompt (its requirements, delivery spec and audio policy a) and to the input assets. Each task is evaluated at three levels: L1 program checks, derived from and and decided by code; L2 task checks, atomic pass/- fail checks that each quote the requirement they enforce as 4 Figure 3. Rubrics go through rounds of model review, which flags over-strict, missing or undecidable checks, and human verification, until no flag holds; since judges never see the input assets, each check states the correct content itself. The final set has 1,449 L1 checks, 12,985 L2 checks (about 54 per task) and 1,195 L3 rubrics. 4. Evaluation Protocol Rollout. Fig. 2c summarizes the protocol. Every rollout runs in fresh Docker sandbox with common rendering toolchain (e.g., Python, Node, headless browser, ffmpeg) and the TTS tool of 3, under one-hour wall-clock budget. All model traffic is logged, so every trajectory, token and tool call is recorded, and each (system, task) has exactly one scored run; runs lost to an infrastructure fault are re-run. Details are in App. C. L1: delivery and program checks. L1 is decided by programs alone; no model is involved. run delivers if it leaves an MP4 that decodes and can be judged; the delivery rate is the share of tasks with such video. Each delivery is then measured (ffprobe, full decode, audio levels, VAD and Whisper language ID) and checked by code against the tasks machine-readable delivery spec and audio policy a: every task checks container and decodability, resolution, frame rate (0.01) and duration within [tmin0.5, tmax+0.5] s. The 205 core tasks add delivered source project, an exact frame count where requires it (54 tasks) and an audible audio stream (peak > 50 dBFS) where labels channel required. Lessons and papers, which all require narration, add an audible audio stream, narration coverage (VAD), narration language (ASR) and the absence of long black or frozen stretches. This gives 1,449 checks per system (1,177 core, 272 lesson and paper). Spec compliance is the share of tasks whose run passes all applicable checks; non-delivery fails them all. For each check judge returns pass, fail, unknown or n/a, with timestamped evidence. Judges score the 12,985 L2 checks (3.4), and we report two metrics. L2 pass pools checks: it is #pass/(#pass+#fail), with unknown and n/a excluded. L2 strict (strict task success) is decided per run: run succeeds if none of its core checks fails and at least one passes; unknown and n/a do not count against it, and non-delivery fails. For example, the Super Mario level run (CG01) has 59 checks; video in which Mario does not grow after touching the mushroom fails the core check growth is discernible after contact, so the run fails L2 strict even if the other 58 pass (L2 pass 98%); strict success is thus far more discriminative. L3: quality. The judge scores each of the five dimensions from 1 to 5 against the tasks own anchors, with reasons, strengths and defects; dimension the judge cannot assess is left unknown and excluded. For CG01, timing and motion (TM) asks whether continuous motion, landings and state changes can be followed with enough time to see key dangers and successes; it scores 1 if key processes are hard to track, 3 if they can be tracked but transitions or holds are awkward, and 5 if key changes are clear and motion serves the task. The overall score is the mean of the five dimensions, not weighted total of L1L3. Delivered-only and no video = 0. Our primary display reports the delivery rate next to delivered-only L2 and L3 scores, which isolate the quality of what was delivered. We also report every metric with no video = 0: non-delivery scores zero on every dimension and fails every check, so reliability and quality combine into one number. Judge panels. Each delivered video is judged independently by three panels, each given the exact task prompt and the rubric but never the system identity. Judges are told that on-screen or narrated self-declarations are not evidence, and that unsampled instants cannot be asserted. J1 (Gemini 4 Argon [20]) and J2 (Gemini 3.8 Flash [19]) watch the full MP4 with sound (4 fps up to 150 s, adaptively lower for longer videos) and judge everything. J3 splits by modality following the check tags: GPT-5.6 Sol [42] judges visual checks and VQ/VA/CL/TM from 24300 sampled frames (up to 1280 px), and Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash [47] judges audio and audio-visual checks and AQ from full-length proxy with the original audio. Audio observations are passed to the vision judge as reference. All three panels contain evaluated models (J1, J2 and J3s vision judge); J3 shares no family with J1/J2. Each panels metrics are computed separately and then averaged; scores are never mixed across panels within metric (3 2,151 run results). Tab. 2 reports the three-panel mean (per panel: App. E). Human preference. To validate the judges we ran blind pairwise study on all 239 tasks. Annotators saw the full prompt and two synchronized players with videos of two systems on the same task, both playable, and chose A, B, tie or both bad by overall quality and adherence. Human preference therefore measures the quality of delivered videos, not delivery. We fit BradleyTerry strengths [6] on decisive votes (Elo scale, geometric mean 1000) with 2,000-sample bootstrap CIs and compare system ranks and pair outcomes with each panel. 5. Experiments Systems. We evaluate nine agent systems from six labs, each in its native harness at the highest available reasoning effort and run fully autonomously, with no follow-up turns and all tool permissions pre-approved (Tab. 2): GPT-6 Astra [43] and GPT-5.6 Sol [42] (Codex CLI [41]), Claude Opus 5.5 [2] and Sonnet 5.5 [3] (Claude Code [1]), Gemini 4 Argon [20] and Gemini 3.8 Flash [19] (Antigravity CLI [18]), DeepSeekV4.1-Flash, version 1017 [16] (DSH, DeepSeeks own harness [15]), Kimi K3 [40] (Kimi Code [39]) and GLM-5.3Flash [61] (ZCode [62]). Agents receive one fixed instruction (Read ENVIRONMENT.md and prompt.txt. Complete 6 only that task autonomously using your native harness before the deadline. . . ). Every multimodal agent system ran all 239 tasks (2,151 rollouts). 5.1. Main results Finding 1. The benchmark is far from solved, and GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 lead clearly. The left half of Tab. 2 describes what systems deliver. L1: Opus is the only system to deliver all 239 videos and passes every program check on 99.6% of tasks; at the other end GLM-5.3-Flash delivers 179 videos and complies with the specification on 66.9%. L2: on delivered videos, item-level pass rates are close to the ceiling (80.597.3%), so single checks rarely fail; what fails is getting all of them right on one task (below). L3: Astra (4.13) and Opus (4.07) lead across the board: they hold the top two overall scores on delivered videos and the top two places on every quality dimension except audio (AQ), where Gemini 4 Argon is second; Gemini 3.8 Flash trails (3.47). Human: blind pairwise preferences between two playable videos confirm this order: Astra (Elo 1242) and Opus (1203) lead, and the human ranking matches delivered L3 almost exactly (Spearman ρ=0.98; only the last two places swap). Yet L2 strict success (no core check fails and at least one passes; missing video fails) spreads systems from 26.6% to 76.3%: even the best system, Opus, fails core requirement on about quarter of tasks. Finding 2. Delivery reliability is second axis, separate from quality. The right half of Tab. 2 counts missing video as failure, and this largely changes both scores and ranks. Astra and Opus deliver almost every video and stay on top, whereas Gemini 4 Argon, which delivers only 77% of its videos, falls from 4th to 7th. Reliability also has quieter forms: 48 of the 213 playable videos of GPT-5.6 Sol have no audio track, which gives it the lowest AQ on delivered videos (3.71); see App. for details. 5.2. Why videos are not delivered We read the records of all 224 runs that ended without playable video and assigned each one main cause (Fig. 4a). Finding 3. Videos are lost to how agents use their time. Three quarters of the failures (169) are final renders that started too late, ran too slowly or never started; the rest are stalled renders (45, 20%), outputs the agent destroyed itself (7, 3%) and other causes (3). Time management. Agents polish components and previews and launch the full render last: GPT-5.6 Sols final full renders in failed runs start at median of 9 minutes before the deadline, often with frame-by-frame browser capture that needs 535 minutes, and across systems 65 runs (31 of them GLM-5.3-Flashs) never start final render at all. Stalled renders occur only in the two Gemini systems: 33 renders deadlock because the agents script pipes frames into ffmpeg while never reading its error stream (one stopped at frame 7,744 of 10,102, about 90 from completion), and in 12 runs the agent ended its turn while render ran in the background, which was then cut off. Self-destruction is the most avoidable: DeepSeek verified its video twice, then re-encoded it in place one minute before the deadline and left truncated 0.26 MB file. The successful systems leave margin. Opus, the only system without failure, finishes its video median of 24 minutes before the deadline, against 1011 minutes for Sol and GLM (Fig. 4b); it first produces complete deliverable, then improves only copies and verifies the encoded MP4 itself. Given longer budget, slower systems recover some of these videos (App. I.3). 5.3. How agents make videos We analyze the 2,151 trajectories (tool calls, written files, commands) to characterize the process. Finding 4. Agents build their own renderers, and selfinspection is universal but not decisive. The pipeline is always code frames ffmpeg: runs call ffmpeg in 96100% of cases, while Manim appears in 8 of 2,151 runs and MoviePy in 13. Each system has preferred rendering stack (Fig. 4c): Claude agents and Gemini 4 Argon draw vectors with cairo (4254%), GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi and GLM rasterize frames with PIL/numpy (43 55%), and Astra, DeepSeek and Gemini 3.8 Flash capture browser canvases and three.js scenes (5260%). Soundtracks are programmed: 5796% of runs synthesize music or effects in code. Cairo and browser-2D runs pass the container-level check most often (88% and 85%) and score highest (3.79 and 3.73), three.js scenes least (78%, 3.00); since renderer and system are coupled, this is an association, consistent with slow frame capture being main cause of late renders (5.2). 95% of runs view their own rendered frames, yet the amount of looking does not predict delivered quality (ρ=0.07, n=9; Fig. 4d): Astra looks least (median 3 images per run) and scores best, while DeepSeek looks most (median 35). Reports often claim verifications that do not hold: among playable videos that fail spec compliance, the final report still claims verification (verified, ffprobe, confirmed) in 10 of 14 for Astra and 3 of 11 for Sol. 5.4. On single pairs the mean agrees with humans 73.3% of the time, but the agreement depends on the margin: 63% when the panels score gap is below 0.2 (about third of pairs) 8 and 86% when it is 0.5 or more. Judges also miss what humans flag: on pairs that annotators label both bad, the panels give the same scores (3.81) as on other pairs, so judge scores order videos but do not certify them as acceptable. Across the nine systems, the rank correlation between mean cost and the overall score is ρ=0.55 (permutation p=0.13). Three systems lie on the costscore Pareto frontier (Fig. 5b): GLM5.3-Flash ($0.32, 2.79), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash ($0.47, 3.91) and GPT-6 Astra ($8.19, 4.11). Output tokens per task range from 61k (Astra) to 289k (Sonnet), and within each system run duration and score are negatively correlated (ρ from 0.22 to 0.69). Costs are list-price equivalents of logged token usage (billing-verified for Claude); per-system details are in App. G. 6. Conclusion We presented VibeVideoBench, 239 realistic, checkable tasks on which multimodal agents make complete audiovisual videos with code, evaluated by program checks, taskspecific rubric checks and quality scores from three judge panels. Across nine frontier agent systems, the benchmark is far from solved: GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 lead, yet the best system satisfies every core requirement on only 76.3% of tasks. Delivery is second axis next to quality: counting missing videos as zero changes the ranking, and most lost videos are final renders that started too late, ran too slowly or never started. The judges system rankings agree with human preferences, while on individual pairs of videos they agree with humans only 73% of the time.

Rubric Design B.1. Structure of rubric Each rubric groups the task checks (L2) under few core goals, maps every requirement of the prompt to the checks that enforce it, and adds the tasks quality rubric (L3), whose five dimensions are anchored at 1, 3 and 5 by descriptions written for that task. check states what passes and what fails, where in the video to look and which prompt sentence it enforces, and carries criticality and modality tag (Tab. B.1). Over the 239 tasks there are 12,985 checks (54.3 per task, 13110); 85.8% are core, the rest detail (supporting for lessons and papers). Unknown is reserved for insufficient evidence: confirmed omissions or violations in the complete work are fail and must not be concealed with unknown. Table B.1. Example task checks from CG01 (Super Mario; 7 core goals, 59 checks). ID / tag Title Pass Fail Observation scope V05 core, visual Initial small form V12 core, visual Large form breaks brick from below V30 core, visual V41 core, visual Complete jumps Order of key events core, V50 audio-visual Jump SFX synchronization Mario is small at departure and does not possess large-form abilities without cause during the initial stage. After becoming large, Mario hits BRICK1 or BRICK2 from below and causes at least one to shatter. Required jumps have traceable takeoff, airborne movement and landing/contact. Q1 mushroom brick G1 stomp shell kicked into G2 hit by G3 lift over pit flagpole and castle. jump cue corresponding to the action is present at each required takeoff. Starts in the large form and skips the first growth, or has already grown before acquiring the mushroom. Breaking the brick early in small form, without contact, or hitting only the question block. From departure until before the first mushroom contact After the transformation until the first brick breaks Pose changes impersonate displacement; teleporting to the landing point. Reordering events, or montage that hides the actual sequence. All required jumps Whole video No cue, or the effect occurs during an unrelated action. Every required takeoff and the audio track Quality rubric. The five L3 dimensions share 20 observation points: 2 3 4 hierarchy organization VQ key-content legibility VA CL TM action AQ intelligibility and pronunciation stability composition key relations state change and transitions prosody occlusion/cropping/layering unity of visual language information load dwell on key content mixing object consistency audience fit channel coordination overall rhythm soundevent alignment Each dimension has task-specific anchors at 1, 3 and 5 (e.g., VQ for CG01: 1 = key content remains unclear or is disrupted by visual defects, 5 = key content clear, image stable, details support viewing); 2 or 4 must say which anchor it is closer to, and insufficient evidence yields unknown, never default 3. Intentional pixel-art style, grain or blur is not defect. B.2. Authoring principles Traceability. Every check quotes the prompt sentence it enforces, and optional language (may, e.g.) never becomes mandatory. Process over claims. correct final number or caption reading synced cannot pass check that requires visible process: in marble adder the sum must be produced by actual contacts. 15 Criticality fixed in advance. Core and detail are fixed before any output is seen, so cosmetic passes cannot outvote failed core goal. Timing under sampling. At least seconds passes only if the lower bound of the sampled interval is , fails if the upper bound is <N , and is otherwise unknown. No prescribed method. 4050 checks is coverage aim, not quota, and no check may prescribe production method. B.3. Rubrics for lessons and papers The 34 lessons and papers (C11, C12) use the same levels and judge interface, but their checks come from the supplied material. L1 adds narration coverage (VAD speech share 50%, no gap over 20 s), narration language (ASR, 90% in the target language) and no long black or frozen stretch. L2 has 4883 checks per task (2,172 in total; 1,566 core): content checks enumerate the knowledge points (each concept, derivation step, worked answer, common misconception and relation to be drawn; for papers the motivation, key idea, method components, key equations, results, evidence and limitations), and narration checks require correct reading of terms, formulas and numbers, explanation rather than reading on-screen text aloud, and synchronization at 46 key moments. Because judges never see the note or the paper, 330 checks that referred to them (consistent with the note) were rewritten to state the required content, and six audit agents re-derived every number and formula against the source. Each task also has grounded quiz (404 questions), reported separately (App. I.2). B.4. Quality control Rubrics were refined over many rounds in closed loop. In each round an independent model reviewed every rubric against its prompt, each finding was re-adjudicated in fresh context and verified by human reviewer, confirmed findings were fixed, and the revised rubrics re-entered review until no confirmed finding remained. The most frequent defect was over-specification (a rubric demanding more than the prompt), ahead of coverage gaps; the review also surfaced bugs in the tasks themselves, such as an infeasible inventory or contradictory timing tables, which were fixed in the prompts. B.5. Modality tags Each check is tagged with the evidence needed to decide it: visual 9,006 (69.4%), audio-visual 3,012 (23.2%) and audio 967 (7.4%). The tags route checks in J3 (App. D). C. The harness prompt is fixed: Read ENVIRONMENT.md and prompt.txt. Complete only that task autonomously using your native harness before the deadline. . . ENVIRONMENT.md states the 3,600 budget, which includes model waits, tools, TTS, previews and the final render. It imposes no token, tool-call or preview limits and lists the deliverables 16 (final MP4, editable project, timing sheet and production notes). It asks the agent to finish with honest verification results. At the deadline the container is killed. D. Judge Protocol and Judge Analysis D.1. Protocol Each judge receives the prompt the agent received, the task checks and the quality rubric, but never the system identity, the source code or the agents notes. For every check it returns pass, fail, unknown or n/a with the time range and the channel (picture or sound) that support the verdict, and it scores the five quality dimensions against the tasks anchors with reasons. On-screen or narrated claims ( requirement met) are not evidence, properties of the delivered file are left to the program checks, judge that sees sampled frames may not assert what happens between them, and insufficient evidence yields unknown. J1 (Gemini 4 Argon) and J2 (Gemini 3.8 Flash) watch the whole video with sound and judge everything. J3 splits the work by modality tag: GPT-5.6 Sol judges the visual checks and VQ, VA, CL and TM from sampled frames, and Qwen3.8-OmniFlash judges the audio and audio-visual checks and AQ from the full video with its original sound. Each of the 1,927 playable videos was judged by all three panels. run without playable video scores zero on every dimension and fails every check (4). Example judge output (J1, CG01, Claude Opus 5.5): CG01-V41 pass. The events occur in exact order: Q1 hit & mushroom power-up (9.015.75 s) brick break (21.0 s) G1 stomp (22.75 s) K1 stomp, kick & G2 defeat (30.2533.0 s) G3 side hit (41.0 s) MOVE1 crossing (47.554.0 s) flagpole & castle (61.7568.5 s). CG01-V50 pass (audio). rising pitch jump sound effect plays synchronously at each of Marios takeoffs (e.g., 6.0 s, 8.75 s, 17.5 s, 20.5 s, . . . , 61.75 s). VQ = 4. Human Preference Study Protocol. Annotators compare two videos made by two systems for the same task. Both videos are playable and judged by all three panels, so the study measures the quality of delivered videos, not delivery. System pairs are balanced across tasks and the sides are randomized; annotators are blind to system identity and judge scores. Ablations Four ablations, each run once per cell after the main evaluation, ask whether the scores can be trusted and whether the setting limited the results: Can the judges see defects? (I.1) Do the scores reflect whether video actually teaches? (I.2) Was one hour enough? (I.3) Did the agents need more CPU cores? (I.4) I.1. Judge stress test We took 30 delivered videos, re-encoded each one cleanly and built ten defective versions with ffmpeg: five picture defects in the window from 35% to 65% of the runtime (black frames, grey box over the center, heavy blur, frozen picture) or over the whole video (leftright mirror), two sound defects (a silent window, another tasks soundtrack), audio delayed by 0.5 or 1.5 s, and the two halves swapped. Apart from the black window, every defective version passes all program checks, so only judge can notice it. J1 judged each video in its clean version and in five of the defects (15 videos per defect, 180 judgments) with the unchanged prompt and rubric, and was not told that anything was injected. Judges see broken pictures but not late sound (Fig. I.1). Every picture defect, the foreign soundtrack and the swapped halves are named in all 15 reports and cost 1.51.9 points on the related dimension; silent window is named in 7 of 15 (0.80 on AQ). Neither audio delay is mentioned in any report, and reports often praise the synchronization; the five-dimension mean drops only slightly (0.11 and 0.16; Wilcoxon p=0.07 and 0.05), spread over several dimensions rather than AQ. Detection does not always reach the checks: mirrored and reordered videos are named in every report, yet most of their target checks still pass (flip rate +4.5 and +14.9 points over clean), and the penalty lands on VQ and CL instead. Finally, the clean re-encode scores +0.12 [+0.03, +0.22] above the original judgment of the same video, so gaps of 0.10.2 between single videos are within judge noise. Audio-visual timing is thus blind spot of both the judges and the program checks, so our rubrics set no strict offset limit: synchronization check asks only that the right sound accompanies the right event (App. B), not that audio and picture align within fixed tolerance. 26 Figure I.1. Judge stress test (J1; 15 videos per defect). Left: share of reports that name the defect (checked by hand). Right: change of the most related L3 dimension against the clean re-encode of the same video (95% bootstrap CI). I.2. Do the videos teach? grounded quiz Each of the 34 lessons and papers has multiple-choice quiz written from its source material (404 questions). plain multiple-choice quiz is not enough: strong model can answer many of these questions from prior knowledge without watching the video, so every answer must point to the moment in the video that supports it. grader (Gemini 4 Argon) watches only the finished video and answers AD or (the video does not cover it). Every AD answer must give timestamp and the videos own words; narration quotes are matched against Whisper transcript and on-screen quotes against the frames, and an answer whose evidence does not check out counts as E. tasks score is its share of correct answers; run without video scores 0. The quiz does not enter the leaderboard. Figure I.2. Grounded quiz on the 34 lessons and papers: share of questions answered correctly (mean over tasks) vs. the three-panel overall on the same tasks (no video = 0). The quiz agrees with the judges. Although it uses neither the rubric nor the quality anchors, its system ranking correlates with the three-panel overall at Spearman ρ=0.93 (Fig. I.2; also 0.93 on playable videos only). The top four systems convey 9396% of the tested points; Gemini 4 Argons 77.4% comes from its five tasks without playable video (90.8% on the other 27 29). Almost no point is lost to wrong answer (2 of 3,425 AD answers); the losses are questions the video does not cover or whose evidence does not check out, so the quiz measures coverage of the material more than correctness. I.3. Time budget We reran DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Gemini 3.8 Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash on 20 tasks with budgets of 15, 30, 60 and 120 minutes (one run per cell, otherwise as in the main evaluation). How much time is enough differs between systems. Flash tends to end its runs on its own well before the deadline, whereas DeepSeek and GLM use the extra time they are given; some GLM runs are still cut at the deadline even with the longest budget, and single GLM call can spend long time reasoning before issuing any tool call. I.4. CPU budget We reran six systems (Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 3.8 Flash, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash, Kimi K3, GPT-5.6 Sol) on the same 20 render-heavy tasks with 2, 8 and 16 CPU cores; the main evaluation uses 8. Everything else is as in the main run; scores are the three-panel mean with no video = 0 (360 runs), compared over the 120 tasksystem pairs. More cores do not measurably help (Fig. I.4). None of the pooled differences is significant (+0.09 for 8 vs. 2 cores, +0.13 for 16 vs. 8, +0.22 for 16 vs. 2; p=0.57, 0.44, 0.20; bootstrap over tasks gives the same conclusion), and playable videos go 28 Figure I.4. CPU budget (6 systems 20 tasks; three-panel mean, no video = 0). Left: mean score per system and setting, with playable videos of all six systems on top. Right: pooled paired difference with 95% CI and paired-t p. from 99 to 101 and 103 of 120 (sign tests p0.56). The systems disagree in direction (Kimi and Flash do best with eight cores, Sol with two, DeepSeek is flat), and delivered quality hardly moves (3.81, 3.84, 3.92). Argons rise from 9 to 12 videos comes mostly from fewer ffmpeg pipe deadlocks in the 16-core arm (2 of its 8 failures there, against 9 of 21 in the other two), which barely use the CPU; render-heavy tasks still run out of time with sixteen cores. The CPU budget therefore does not measurably limit the main results. J. Limitations and Broader Impact Limitations. Fixed budget. Every run gets one hour. Longer budgets, which may let agents make better videos, are left to future work. Adherence over creativity. The rubrics mainly measure whether video follows its specification. Creativity and originality enter only partly, through the aesthetics dimension (VA), and are not evaluated on their own. Judge dependence. All panels are proprietary models, and the judges are insensitive to audio-visual timing (App. I.1). Rankings are stable across the three panels, but absolute values are panel-specific and are never mixed. Coverage. The task set is mostly English (209 of 239) and limited to 1080p-class outputs. Tasks with very long runtimes are few. Broader impact. Code-driven video makes precise, editable and accessible content (lessons, data stories, instructions) cheaper to produce, and our findings point to concrete reliability improvements. Risks include persuasive marketing content and misinformation rendered with an appearance of precision. Tasks with factual content ship their facts as inputs and forbid fabricated claims (e.g., do not claim real interception probability). No task depicts real private individuals. Classic-game tasks use newly designed levels and assets in recognizable style for research evaluation; we will not redistribute original game assets. 29 K.
